incumbent_reading: The paper holds that MCCL's firearms examiners kept their method because court challenges to firearms evidence were distant, while its toxicologists changed their reporting because a challenge was imminent in their own jurisdiction, so that locally immediate routes give more impetus to local change than remote ones (C03; F84, F87, F88, F160, F161, all in the author's voice).

wager.statement:
Re-attribute what separated the two units. The paper credits distance: remote for firearms, immediate for toxicology. A second thing varied across the pair and is printed on one side only: a change already being worked toward under a standing requirement.

Before the NAS report the laboratory was adapting to ISO 17025 and the toxicology unit had a multi-year plan to estimate measurement uncertainty (F98). State law and ASCLD required a five-percent confidence range for blood-alcohol measurement, the protocol already logged instruments, reagents and standards, and the laboratory was reporting at a 95% confidence level while preparing fuller uncertainty estimates for ISO compliance (F101). When the local challenge became imminent the unit accelerated that plan and prepared the statistical analysis (F98). At an outreach session for criminal-justice personnel Jason rejected the idea that the laboratory had only begun uncertainty work because of the NAS report, cited ISO and NIST requirements, and said the new calculation used several years of existing quality-control data (F102). The paper's own table puts ASCLD accreditation standards in toxicology's professional-association cell (F143, author's account) and identifies no professional-association route for firearms (F142, author's account).

On the firearms side no fragment prints a plan for the unit, and none says what the laboratory's ISO 17025 adaptation (F98) asked of it. The one professional-body response printed on the firearms criticism is a rebuttal: AFTE leaders issued a detailed rebuttal to parts of the NAS criticism of firearms work (F78). IAI and AFTE also answered the report with selected rebuttals and commitments to have their research committees study the recommendations further (F35). One examiner's work, at least, had been under outside review: Adam says outsiders had repeatedly reviewed his work without challenging it (F66).

Read this way, the pair does not set a unit that changed beside a unit that did not. It sets a unit whose change was already planned and required beside a unit with no plan and no requirement of its own in print, and the imminent challenge brought the plan forward. The wager is that the standing requirement is what made the difference, and that the immediate route accounts for when toxicology's reports changed, not for the fact that they did. A requirement met on a multi-year plan is hard to count among C03's locally immediate routes, so on this reading the pair shows the slower route doing the work.

This sits close to C17, which already lists accreditation work under way, and to F161, where the author's account has that work making the change easier. It parts from C03, which takes this pair to show that immediacy supplies the impetus.

what_it_would_take_to_cohere.observation: The timetable of the toxicology unit's multi-year plan as it stood before the local challenge, meaning when uncertainty estimates were due to enter reports, set against when they did; and whether the laboratory's ISO 17025 adaptation placed any requirement on the firearms unit.
what_it_would_take_to_cohere.basis: Not in the record. F98 prints that the plan was multi-year, predated the NAS report and was accelerated, but gives neither its original date nor how far it was brought forward. F101 and F102 print what the plan drew on, not when it was due. For firearms I read every fragment for that unit (F10, F14, F18, F22, F26, F29, F59 to F82, F84 to F87, F160, F171, and the Table 2 cells F130, F133, F136, F139, F142, F145, F148, F151), together with F83, a narcotics analyst speaking about firearms, F164 from the discussion, and the laboratory-wide fragments F36, F57 and F98. F98 has the laboratory adapting to ISO 17025 without saying what that asked of the firearms unit, no fragment prints a plan for firearms, and F142 records that the paper's table identifies no professional-association route for that unit. F33 and F34 print field-wide responses from AAFS and ASCLD without naming a unit. The corpus does not say why the timetable is not given.

strains_against: F98 -- two things in the stub that carries the reading. It prints that the unit accelerated the plan when the challenge became imminent, so immediacy can be moved from whether to when but stays in the episode and may have done more than the reading allows. And it has the laboratory, not the toxicology unit alone, adapting to ISO 17025 before the report; if that adaptation reached the firearms unit, that unit also stood under a requirement and did not change, and the variable the reading credits would not separate the two.

F90 -- a local defense attorney planned the challenge in an MCCL case and intended to bring in an outside engineering expert; the acceleration follows a concrete local event, which is the order C03 expects.

F81 -- the author's account is that the challenges to firearms evidence had not succeeded in excluding it, while F90 has the toxicology attack already winning DUI cases elsewhere; the record of the challenge also varied across the pair, and a challenge known to win could carry the difference without either distance or a standing requirement.

F103 -- the new reports state a narrow range at a 99% confidence level, where F101 has the laboratory previously reporting at 95%; if the plan did not already specify that level, the challenge shaped what changed as well as when, and the corpus does not say which.

F80 -- a firearms examiner who drew lessons from defense questioning urged colleagues to answer criticism and not dismiss it, and the author's gloss (p. 635) treats examiners with direct admissibility-hearing experience as more motivated toward field change; exposure moves at least what examiners say, where no plan or requirement is printed.

F153 -- outside the pair, narcotics had a professional-association route (F144, author's account) and is recorded as not changing; the reading holds only if what counted for toxicology was a requirement with a plan behind it (F98, F101), since the narcotics discussion is printed as considering a requirement (F124), not imposing one.

F33 -- AAFS and ASCLD supported the NAS recommendations and promoted actions such as universal laboratory accreditation and analyst certification; that is association pressure toward requirements on laboratories and analysts in general, the firearms unit not excepted.

F34 -- ASCLD advised laboratory leaders to ready staff for courtroom questions and to establish the reliability of their analyses; with F33, an association route to the firearms unit is in print in a general form, and the difference the reading credits narrows to whether a specific requirement and plan existed.

F67 -- firearms examiners contrast an earlier reliance on intuitive recognition with a current expectation of documented images; some change in how that unit backs its reports and testimony had happened by an undated point, so 'no plan in print' describes the record and may not describe the unit.
wager.who_could_complete_it: Whoever held the laboratory's accreditation timetable, such as unit supervisors, the laboratory director or the deputy director, or the laboratory's ISO 17025 planning documents from before the report, including whatever they asked of the firearms unit.

fragment_jobs.F87: Gives the paper's fuller firearms account, in which distance is combined with incompatible technique and affronted values, which shows the pair never varied distance alone.
fragment_jobs.F160: Summarizes the firearms side in the author's voice and is the side of the pair on which the reading finds no plan and no requirement specific to the unit printed.
fragment_jobs.F88: States the incumbent attribution in the author's voice, that the anticipated challenge created the reason to change, and is set against F98's prior plan.
fragment_jobs.F98: Carries the reading: it dates the uncertainty plan before the NAS report and prints the challenge as accelerating that plan, which the paper uses as support for immediacy and the reading uses to separate the direction of the change from its timing; its acceleration clause and its laboratory-wide ISO clause are both declared as strains.
fragment_jobs.F161: Is where the author's account itself says the court threat was aligned with accreditation work already under way and that this made the change easier; the reading promotes that clause from easing condition to difference-maker.
fragment_jobs.F101: Shows a numerical requirement from state law and ASCLD, and reporting at a 95% level, in place before the challenge, so that the unit was already working inside a standing requirement.
fragment_jobs.F102: Gives a toxicologist's own account, at an outreach session for criminal-justice personnel, of where the work came from (ISO and NIST requirements, several years of existing quality-control data) together with his rejection of the report as its origin; the reading takes the plan's existence from F98 and F101 and uses this as his account.
fragment_jobs.F143: Is the paper's own listing of accreditation standards as a route for toxicology, which lets the re-attribution be made inside the paper's table.
fragment_jobs.F142: Is the paper's own record that no professional-association route is identified for firearms, the other side of the variable the reading credits.
fragment_jobs.F78: Prints the one professional-body response that is specific to the firearms criticism, a detailed rebuttal, where toxicology's side prints a requirement.
fragment_jobs.F35: Prints IAI and AFTE answering the report with selected rebuttals and commitments to further study; AFTE is the body F78 has rebutting the firearms criticism.
fragment_jobs.F66: Has an examiner who appears in the unit's technical review (F69) reporting that outsiders repeatedly reviewed his own work without challenging it; the reading sets this beside the absence of any printed requirement on the unit, since review of his work is printed and a demand arising from it is not.
fragment_jobs.F90: Declared strain: prints the planned local challenge and the outside expert, the concrete event after which the unit accelerated, and the attack's record of winning cases elsewhere.
fragment_jobs.F81: Declared strain: with F90 it shows the record of the challenge varying across the pair, won elsewhere for toxicology and, on the author's account, not successful for firearms.
fragment_jobs.F103: Declared strain: prints the 99% confidence level of the new reports, which may mean the challenge shaped the content of the change.
fragment_jobs.F80: Declared strain: prints a firearms examiner urging colleagues to answer criticism, with the author's gloss tying such motivation to direct hearing experience.
fragment_jobs.F153: Declared strain: records narcotics as unchanged although the table gives it a professional-association route.
fragment_jobs.F144: Is the table's cell giving narcotics a professional-association route through the SWG-DRUG debate, which the reading has to distinguish from a standing requirement.
fragment_jobs.F124: Prints the SWG-DRUG discussion as considering a requirement, which is the basis for distinguishing a debate from a requirement already in force.
fragment_jobs.F33: Declared strain: prints AAFS and ASCLD promoting universal laboratory accreditation and analyst certification, association pressure that is not confined to one unit.
fragment_jobs.F34: Declared strain: prints ASCLD's general advice to laboratory leaders, an association route that is not confined to toxicology.
fragment_jobs.F67: Declared strain: prints an undated earlier change in how firearms examiners back their reports, so the unit is not without change in print.

grounded_in.how: F98 prints a plan that predates the NAS report and was accelerated when the challenge became imminent; F88, in the author's voice, has the anticipated challenge creating the reason for toxicologists to change their reporting. One has the challenge altering the pace of a change already planned; the other has it supplying the reason for the change.

grounded_in.question: When was the multi-year plan due to put uncertainty estimates into reports, and how far did the imminent challenge bring that forward?
grounded_in.if_one_way: If the plan was due at about the time the reports did change, C03's toxicology case would read as a scheduled change that an immediate challenge barely moved, and the pair would not show immediacy producing change.
grounded_in.if_the_other: If the plan was years from delivery or had no reporting date, C03 would read as the paper states it: the immediate local route turned preparation into practice.

grounded_in.question: Did the laboratory's ISO 17025 adaptation (F98) place any requirement on the firearms unit?
grounded_in.if_one_way: If it placed a comparable requirement on firearms and that unit still did not change, C03 would read as stated, because the two units would then differ in the distance of their challenges and not in having a requirement.
grounded_in.if_the_other: If it asked nothing of firearms, C03's contrast would read as confounded: the units differed in whether any standing requirement existed, and distance could not be credited separately.

rival: The paper's own account at full strength: a plan is not a practice. The unit accelerated and delivered once a challenge was planned in an MCCL case (F90, F98), and firearms, with no such case reaching local testimony (F84, author's account), changed nothing. The prior accreditation work lowered the cost, which C17 and F161 already say. On that reading the re-attribution is a shift of emphasis inside what the paper credits and is not needed.

drift: The F153 fragment job says it 'records narcotics as unchanged although the table gives it a professional-association route.' F153 explicitly reports the author's account of no local change. Presenting that characterization as a recorded outcome drops its attribution. This is drift, not an additional import kill.
verdicts.note: KILL. The imported factual separation is: 'A second thing varied across the pair and is printed on one side only: a change already being worked toward under a standing requirement.' F98, F101 and F102 carry the toxicology plan, compliance work and requirements. No fragment carries the assertion that this condition actually varied between the two units. F98 describes laboratory-wide ISO adaptation without specifying its firearms implications; F142 carries only the author's table's omission of a direct professional-association spillover route, not the absence of a firearms requirement or plan. The later, narrower wording 'no plan and no requirement of its own in print' accurately describes a documentary asymmetry, but cannot establish the opening assertion of a difference between the units. That unprinted separation is what the reading credits when it says 'the standing requirement is what made the difference.' The card itself identifies whether ISO imposed a firearms requirement as an unanswered question. Declaring that uncertainty does not supply the factual separation asserted in the statement. This kill concerns the conversion of unequal documentation into an actual difference, not merely the proposal of an alternative causal interpretation.

considered_not_fired.item: Pre-existing toxicology preparation and acceleration: statement and fragment jobs F98, F101 and F102.
considered_not_fired.why: F98 explicitly places the multi-year uncertainty plan before the NAS report and says the imminent local challenge accelerated it and prompted the statistical analysis. F101 carries the logged instruments, reagents and standards, the state-law and ASCLD five-percent requirement, prior 95-percent reporting and preparation for ISO compliance. F102 carries Jason's outreach setting, rejection of a NAS-only origin, ISO/NIST references and use of existing quality-control data. These details are supported paraphrases; Jason's explanation remains attributed to him.

considered_not_fired.item: The narrower assertion that no firearms change plan or unit-specific ISO requirement is printed.
considered_not_fired.why: The corpus does not specify such a plan or ISO obligation. F98 leaves the firearms implications of laboratory-wide adaptation unspecified. F33 and F34 describe general association responses, F36 directs staff to read the report, and F57 concerns staff movement. F67 prints a documentation expectation, which the card separately acknowledges. None supplies the missing firearms counterpart to the toxicology uncertainty plan. The documentary absence itself is not an import; treating it as an established between-unit difference is the kill identified above.

considered_not_fired.item: Author-attributed accounts in fragment jobs F84, F87, F88, F160 and F161, and the statement's table references F142 and F143.
considered_not_fired.why: The cited fragments carry the author's distance explanation, firearms technique/value incompatibility, local toxicology impetus and accreditation work easing change. F142 and F143 carry the table's respective pathway entries. The card generally marks these as the author's account or the paper's table. Using or disputing those printed explanations is not itself importing evidence.

considered_not_fired.item: Professional-body responses and outside review: F78, F35 and F66 fragment jobs.
considered_not_fired.why: F78 prints AFTE's detailed rebuttal; F35 prints IAI/AFTE rebuttals and commitments to further study. Read together, the card does not suppress the study commitment when describing the firearms-specific rebuttal. F66 carries Adam's report of repeated outside review without challenge, and F69 independently places Adam in the technical-review episode. No reviewer identity, new demand or review consequence is invented.

considered_not_fired.item: Challenge sequence and potentially different change content: fragment jobs F90, F81, F103 and F80.
considered_not_fired.why: F90 carries successful DUI attacks elsewhere, the planned local challenge and intended outside expert. F81 carries the explicitly attributed author account of unsuccessful firearms exclusion challenges. F103 carries the new 99-percent confidence level. F80 carries the examiner's appeal to answer criticism, while its gloss supplies the separately attributed link to direct hearing experience. The suggestion that the challenge may have shaped report content is conditional, not a claim that an unprinted event occurred.

considered_not_fired.item: Narcotics comparison and broader pressures: fragment jobs F153, F144, F124, F33, F34 and F67.
considered_not_fired.why: F144 carries the table's SWG-DRUG pathway and F124 explicitly describes a requirement under consideration, supporting the distinction from an imposed change requirement. F33 and F34 carry general accreditation advocacy and courtroom-preparation advice. F67 carries the earlier-to-current shift toward documented images without dating it. F153's attribution loss is recorded as drift, not import.

considered_not_fired.item: The proposal that immediacy affected timing, and the comparison with C17.
considered_not_fired.why: F98 supplies a printed basis for separating a prior plan from its acceleration. Offering that distinction as a causal wager is not independently killed merely because the author prefers another account. The card explicitly leaves the original reporting timetable and the firearms ISO obligation unresolved. Its acknowledged proximity to C17 and F161 is not a reason to reinstate the retired incumbent-equivalence kill.

verdicts.note: CLEAR. All 172 fragment stubs were examined, with fragment notes and the absence register. No fragment outside the seeds and declared strains requires an event or practice incompatible with the reading. The B failure is an unsupported assertion of between-unit variation; the record does not positively establish the opposite variation, so it does not also fire E. Author explanations, including those explicitly identified as such within stubs, establish what the author claims rather than independently establishing the disputed causal relation.

considered_not_fired.why: These are explicitly declared strains, and F98 is also a seed. They cover acceleration following the local challenge, laboratory-wide ISO adaptation, the challenges' different success records, the new confidence level, firearms responsiveness and documentation change, general association pressure and narcotics nonchange. They therefore cannot supply an undeclared-contradiction kill.

The reading accommodates the local toxicology threat, its immediacy and its alignment with existing work. It disputes whether that threat explains change itself or its timing. The causal priority in these fragments is the author's explanation; no additional printed event here establishes that the prior plan could not have led to reporting change.

The firearms preference for holistic judgment, limited CMS use, rejection of percentage-style matches and technical/value incompatibility are additional features the reading can accommodate. The F87 job explicitly recognizes that distance was not the pair's only difference. None establishes a firearms uncertainty-change plan or corresponding standing obligation that would contradict the card's narrower claim about what is printed. The author's causal weighting of values and technique is not an event-level refutation.

Firearms technical review, documentation, training, an available numerical identification method and a management instruction to read the NAS report are printed. They are not a plan or standing requirement to make the reporting change at issue. The card's contextual claim about a missing counterpart to the toxicology plan need not deny routine obligations or review practices.

Toxicologists' enthusiasm and the table's changed/unchanged contrast remain compatible with the reading. Its phrase 'the pair does not set a unit that changed beside a unit that did not' introduces a different explanation of the contrast; the F84 job explicitly retains the firearms outcome, and the statement repeatedly acknowledges toxicology's changed reports. It does not require denying those outcomes.

Narcotics has existing verification obligations, workload constraints, a feared future prohibition, a discussed confirmation requirement and possible camera adaptation. These do not print an imposed requirement plus a prior plan for the particular change being debated. The card does not claim that every obligation or every association route must produce change, and it declares narcotics nonchange as a strain.

considered_not_fired.item: F62, F79, F82, DG03 and A01; the missing toxicology timetable and firearms ISO scope.
considered_not_fired.why: Meeting reports establish criticism, frustration and discussion among firearms examiners, not an unacknowledged local implementation outcome. DG03 and A01 expressly state that the author lacks data on what externally challenged examiners did in their own laboratories. The toxicology timetable and firearms ISO scope are likewise unspecified in the supplied record. Missing evidence cannot become a contradicting stub.

attack.kept: A killed reading is retained, marked. Deleting it removes the evidence that the pass functions.
